content: The following are potential adverse effects or conditions associated with the use of oral contraceptives, including ethynodiol diacetate and ethinyl estradiol: 1. Edema: Swelling due to fluid retention may occur. 2. Chloasma or Melasma: Hyperpigmentation of the skin, which may persist even after discontinuation of the medication. 3. Breast Changes: These may include tenderness, enlargement, or secretion. 4. Weight Changes: Both weight gain and weight loss have been reported. 5. Cervical Changes: Alterations in cervical erosion or secretion may occur. 6. Lactation Suppression: When administered immediately postpartum, a reduction in milk production and quality may be observed. 7. Cholestatic Jaundice: A condition characterized by yellowing of the skin and eyes due to bile flow obstruction. 8. Migraine: Severe headaches may develop or worsen. 9. Allergic Rash: Skin reactions such as rashes may occur. 10. Mental Depression: Mood changes, including depression, have been reported. 11. Reduced Carbohydrate Tolerance: Impaired glucose metabolism may be observed. 12. Vaginal Candidiasis: Yeast infections of the vagina may occur. 13. Corneal Changes: Steepening of the corneal curvature, which may lead to contact lens intolerance. 14. Contact Lens Intolerance: Difficulty wearing contact lenses due to changes in the eye. Additional adverse reactions or conditions reported in users of oral contraceptives, though their association has not been definitively confirmed or refuted, include: 1. Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS): Symptoms such as mood swings, bloating, and irritability. 2. Cataracts: Clouding of the eye lens. 3. Appetite Changes: Increased or decreased appetite. 4. Cystitis-like Syndrome: Symptoms resembling bladder inflammation. 5. Headache: General headaches not classified as migraines. 6. Nervousness: Feelings of anxiety or restlessness. 7. Dizziness: Episodes of lightheadedness or vertigo. 8. Hirsutism: Excessive hair growth in areas where hair is typically minimal. 9. Scalp Hair Loss: Thinning or loss of hair on the scalp. 10. Erythema Multiforme: A skin condition characterized by red, target-like lesions. 11. Erythema Nodosum: Painful, red nodules under the skin. 12. Hemorrhagic Eruption: Skin eruptions associated with bleeding. 13. Vaginitis: Inflammation or infection of the vagina. 14. Porphyria: A group of disorders affecting the skin or nervous system due to enzyme deficiencies. 15. Impaired Renal Function: Reduced kidney function. 16. Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome: A condition causing kidney failure and low red blood cell counts. 17. Acne: Development or worsening of acne. 18. Libido Changes: Increased or decreased sexual desire. 19. Colitis: Inflammation of the colon. 20. Budd-Chiari Syndrome: A rare condition involving blood clots in the liver's veins. 21. Endocervical Hyperplasia or Ectropion: Changes in the cervical lining. Postmarketing Experience There is limited information available regarding the postmarketing experience of ethynodiol diacetate and ethinyl estradiol. Drug Interactions The concurrent use of rifampin has been associated with reduced contraceptive efficacy and an increased incidence of breakthrough bleeding and menstrual irregularities. Similar, though less pronounced, effects have been suggested with barbiturates, phenylbutazone, phenytoin sodium, and possibly with griseofulvin, ampicillin, and tetracyclines. Co-administration of troglitazone with combination oral contraceptives (estrogen and progestin) has been shown to reduce plasma concentrations of both hormones by approximately 30%, potentially compromising contraceptive effectiveness. Use in Specific Populations 1. Pregnancy: There is no FDA or Australian guidance on the use of ethynodiol diacetate and ethinyl estradiol during pregnancy. 2. Labor and Delivery: No FDA guidance exists regarding use during labor and delivery. 3. Nursing Mothers: Small amounts of oral contraceptive steroids have been detected in breast milk, and adverse effects on the child, such as jaundice and breast enlargement, have been reported. Oral contraceptives may also interfere with lactation by reducing the quantity and quality of breast milk. Nursing mothers should be advised to use alternative contraception until weaning is complete. 4. Pediatric Use: Safety and efficacy have been established in women of reproductive age, including postpubertal adolescents under 16 years old. Use before menarche is not indicated. 5. Geriatric Use: There is no FDA guidance on the use of these medications in elderly populations. 6. Gender: No specific FDA guidance exists regarding use in specific gender populations. 7. Race: No specific FDA guidance exists regarding use in specific racial populations. 8. Renal Impairment: No FDA guidance exists for use in patients with renal impairment. 9. Hepatic Impairment: No FDA guidance exists for use in patients with hepatic impairment. 10. Females of Reproductive Potential and Males: No specific FDA guidance exists for these populations. 11. Immunocompromised Patients: No FDA guidance exists for use in immunocompromised individuals. Administration and Monitoring Administration: Oral administration is the recommended route. Monitoring: Limited information is available regarding monitoring requirements for these medications. IV Compatibility There is limited information regarding the compatibility of ethynodiol diacetate and ethinyl estradiol with intravenous administration. Overdosage Overdosage may result in nausea, and withdrawal bleeding may occur in females.
